screens.title: Project 2 — The ALU and Memory
screens.narratorSegment: In this project you will produce the pieces that actually compute and retain data in the Hack computer. You will construct arithmetic components—half adder, full adder, a 16-bit adder and incrementer—and then assemble the ALU, which maps six control bits to eighteen functions. You will also build the memory hierarchy: a 1-bit storage element up through registers and layered R A M chips, finishing with RAM16K as the machine's data memory, and a program counter to sequence instructions. This work is central because it turns logic gates into operations and storage that together run programs. A concrete example: using the ALU you will implement addition and subtraction, and using the R A M chips you will store values that instructions read and update. A common misconception is that memory is a single monolithic block; in this project you will see how each level is constructed from the previous one and why that recursion matters for reliability and testability. By the end you’ll test every ALU function and verify read/write isolation across R A M addresses, and reflect on why sequential design requires a different mindset than combinational design.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Project 2 Overview

Project 2 — The ALU and Memory

Build arithmetic units and a recursive memory tree that together form the Hack computer's working core.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

You will design the ALU and all memory chips, test every ALU function, and verify RAM read/write isolation. Expect combinational and sequential challenges and a final reflection comparing them.

Why it matters

These components turn logic into computation and storage. They are the pieces that let programs compute, remember state, and control flow.

Concept map
ALU
Six control bits choose among arithmetic and logic functions and produce zero/negative flags.
Memory
Built recursively from a single bit up to RAM16K; supports controlled reads and writes.
PC
A sequential counter with load and reset that sequences program execution.
Complete the HDL, run the hardware simulator tests, keep a debugging log, and prepare a reflection on combinational vs sequential design.
Visual preview
ALU pipeline
Pre-process → Function → Post-process → Flags
Memory tree
Bit → Register → RAM8 → ... → RAM16K
Test strategy
Exhaust the ALU's 18 functions and verify RAM read-after-write behavior and address isolation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide your lab work and tests. First, you will complete Project 2 end-to-end: write HDL for every named chip, simulate it, and fix failing tests until each chip passes the provided scripts. Second, you will build the ALU and the memory chips—from the single Bit up to RAM16K—and you will show how each level composes into the next. Third, you'll verify hardware behavior: exhaust the ALU's 18 functions in the simulator and exercise R A M read/write patterns so you can prove address isolation and correct data persistence. Fourth, you will understand roles: know how the ALU implements operations and flags and how memory plus the program counter support the von Neumann execution model. Each objective emphasizes a skill: writing HDL, composing modules, testing with the simulator, and reasoning about sequential versus combinational design. A common pitfall is rushing to the largest chips without unit testing smaller blocks first; instead, verify each primitive and record your discoveries in a debugging log. These objectives prepare you both to build reliable hardware and to reason about why the components behave as they do.

screens.title: Milestones and Tests
screens.narratorSegment: Project work is safest when broken into verifiable milestones. Start by implementing and testing primitive arithmetic chips: HalfAdder and FullAdder. Move to 16-bit combinational modules: Add16 and Inc16, verifying carry propagation and increment edge cases. Implement the ALU last among combinational chips because it integrates many behaviors—verify all 18 functions listed in the specification table. For sequential work, implement Bit and then compose Register. Build RAM8 from Registers, then combine RAM8 units to form RAM64, RAM512, RAM4K and finally RAM16K. For the PC, check three behaviors: incrementing, loading a value when load is asserted, and resetting when reset is asserted. Testing strategy examples: for R A M, verify an uninitialized read returns 0, and that writing at one address does not alter other addresses. For the ALU, exercise combinations that produce zero and negative flags to validate status computation. A misconception to avoid is skipping unit tests for small chips; issues in large assemblies frequently trace back to an untested primitive. Track each passing test as a milestone toward project completion.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Milestones & Tests

Checkpoint plan
Combinational

screens.title: Project 2: Component List and Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Project 2 names thirteen chips split into arithmetic and sequential groups. On the arithmetic side you will implement HalfAdder, FullAdder, Add16 and Inc16, and then integrate them into the ALU. Each smaller adder teaches a concrete idea: the HalfAdder shows how two bits sum and produce a carry; the FullAdder adds a carry input and demonstrates ripple carry when chained to form Add16. Inc16 reuses adder logic to perform a plus-one operation efficiently. The ALU then combines preprocessing and two function choices to produce complex behaviors. On the sequential side you will implement Bit and compose it into a 16-bit Register, then build RAM8 and grow it recursively through RAM64, RAM512, RAM4K to RAM16K. The PC is a small sequential special case that must increment, load, and reset correctly. A practical example: when you test RAM8, write the value 0b0000000000000011 to address 3 and then read it back; the value must persist only at address 3. A common misconception is that registers and R A M behave like immutable storage; in reality they hold state across clock cycles and require explicit load control to avoid unintentional overwrites. As you work, think of each chip as a contract: a precise HDL interface and tests that confirm the contract.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Component Roles
Arithmetic chips
HalfAdder
Sum two bits and produce carry. Fundamental building block.
FullAdder
Adds three bits: two inputs and a carry-in; chainable to create Add16.
Add16 / Inc16
16-bit ripple-carry adder and incrementer built from FullAdders.
ALU
Most complex combinational chip. Implements 18 functions from 6 control bits and returns zero/negative flags.
Sequential chips
Bit / Register
A Bit stores one value across clock ticks; 16 Bits form a Register with load control.
RAM hierarchy
RAM8 built from Registers, repeated to form larger RAMs up to RAM16K in a tree-like composition.
PC
Program counter with increment, load, and reset behaviors to control instruction flow.
Concrete example

Write the value 3 to address 3 in RAM8 and then read it back. Confirm other addresses remain zero. This verifies address decoding and write isolation.

Key Takeaway

Build primitives first; their correctness ensures larger modules work predictably.

screens.title: The ALU Specification
screens.narratorSegment: The ALU is specified as a table mapping six control bits to a set of functions and two status flags. The control bits are labeled zx, nx, zy, ny, f and no. These bits guide a three-stage computation: pre-process inputs x and y (zero and/or negate them), select a function (add or bitwise and), then post-process the result (possible negation). The ALU must also set zr if the output is zero and ng if the output is negative. Practically, this means each control combination implements a distinct arithmetic or logic operation such as zero, one, negative one, x, y, x+1, y-1, x-y and so on. A concrete example from the specification is the use of zx=1, nx=1, zy=1, ny=1, f=1, no=1 to produce the constant 1. A common misconception is to think the ALU has many separate circuits for each function; instead it reuses stages and input manipulation to cover many operations with the same hardware. When you build the ALU, focus on implementing the pre-processing controls correctly and verifying the table rows one by one in the simulator. Each passing row is strong evidence your composition matches the specification.

keyIdea.title: Specification-driven design
keyIdea.text: The ALU's power comes from reuse: six control bits plus preprocessing and postprocessing yield many functions with a single data path.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › ALU Specification
ALU

Six control bits define 18 functions

Understand how zx, nx, zy, ny, f and no are combined to produce output and flags.

Status: produce zr and ng
Pre-/Post-processing
  • zx, zy: replace operand with zero when set.
  • nx, ny: bitwise negate the operand when set.
  • no: negate the final output when set.
Function select
f chooses between bitwise AND (f=0) and arithmetic addition (f=1). Combined with preprocessing, this yields the full set of specified functions.
Specification example
// One test vector example
x = 0b0000000000000010
y = 0b0000000000000001
// control bits to compute x + y
zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=0 f=1 no=0
// expected out = 0b0000000000000011
Common misconception

The ALU is not a collection of many independent circuits; it reuses preprocessing and a small function unit to cover many behaviors.

Key Takeaway

Implement and verify each table row in the simulator. Each passing row confirms correct preprocessing and function selection.

screens.title: ALU Pre-processing Stage
screens.narratorSegment: The ALU's pre-processing stage prepares inputs so a single function unit can produce many outcomes. The controls zx and zy force x or y to zero, which is useful when you want constants like zero, one, or negative one. The nx and ny bits negate the corresponding input, flipping every bit. Together these four bits let you compute complements, prepare operands for two's complement arithmetic, and create constant results without separate logic. For example, to produce -1 you can zero both inputs then negate the result appropriately through post-processing. A concrete example: to compute x - y using two's complement math, you will flip y with ny and use addition in the next stage; the pre-processing produces ~y so the function stage can add x and ~y. A common misunderstanding is that pre-processing merely cleans inputs; instead it encodes arithmetic tricks into operand transforms, enabling subtraction, increments, and constants with minimal hardware. When implementing this stage in HDL, be rigorous: write unit tests that assert the transformed x and y values for combinations of zx, nx, zy and ny so any mistake is caught before the function unit is exercised.

keyIdea.title: Transform before compute
keyIdea.text: Pre-processing encodes operand tricks like negation and zeroing so the ALU's single function unit can implement many operations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › ALU Pre-processing
Pre-processing

Zero and negate inputs

Apply zx/zy and nx/ny to produce modified operands used by the function stage.

Zeroing (zx / zy)
Replaces an entire operand with zero, enabling constants and simpler downstream logic.
Negation (nx / ny)
Bitwise complement flips bits; used to form two's complement operations when combined with addition.
Worked example
Suppose x = 5 and y = 2. To compute x - y via two's complement, set ny=1 to produce ~y, then use addition in the function stage. The pre-processing turns y into ~2 so the function stage can add x and ~y. Correct post-processing then yields the expected negative or positive result depending on the carry conventions of the ALU.
Misconception

Pre-processing is not optional cosmetic wiring; incorrect input transforms are the most common source of functional errors in the ALU.

Check your implementation
  • Unit-test zeroing and negation individually.
  • Verify combinations that produce constants like 0, 1, -1.
Key Takeaway

Correct preprocessing enables many ALU functions with a single function unit; test it thoroughly before moving on.

screens.title: Function and Post-processing Stages
screens.narratorSegment: After pre-processing, the ALU must pick a function and possibly negate the result. The function bit f selects between arithmetic addition and bitwise AND. Addition composes the prepared operands into arithmetic results; AND performs bitwise masking operations. The post-processing control no negates the final output when needed, enabling further variety from a single data path. Equally important are the status flags: zr is set when the final output equals zero, and ng is set when the most significant bit is 1, indicating a negative two's complement number. For example, to produce a logical AND of original x and y, ensure zx and zy are cleared and f is 0; the result will reflect the bitwise intersection of the inputs. A common mistake is computing flags on the pre-processed value instead of the post-processed output; flags must reflect the value presented to the rest of the machine. When you implement this stage, add tests that check flag outcomes for edge cases like zero, negative one, and overflow-like patterns. Affirming flags are correct is crucial because later instruction logic depends on them for branches and comparisons.

keyIdea.title: One data path, many results
keyIdea.text: Function selection plus post-processing and flags turn a single arithmetic/logic unit into a rich operation set relied on by instructions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Function & Post-process
Function stage

Add vs AND, then final negation

Function select (f)

f=0 selects bitwise AND; f=1 selects addition. The inputs are already transformed by the pre-processing stage, so these operations cover many logical and arithmetic behaviors.

Post-processing (no) & flags

If no=1 the output is negated. Compute zr if final out==0 and ng if most significant bit is 1. Flags must reflect the post-processed value used by the CPU for control decisions.

Example test
// Test for logical AND
x = 0b1010101010101010
y = 0b1100110011001100
// controls: zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=0 f=0 no=0
// expected out = bitwise AND of x and y
// flags: zr=false if result nonzero, ng depends on MSB
Pitfall

Calculating flags before applying no yields incorrect flag values. Always compute flags from the final output.

Key Takeaway

Ensure the function unit and post-processing feed the flag logic; test both output values and flags together.

screens.title: Subtraction and Two's Complement Trick
screens.narratorSegment: A classic insight in Project 2 is implementing subtraction with addition through two's complement. The mathematical identity x - y = x + (~y + 1) means we can compute subtraction by flipping y's bits and adding one. The Hack ALU lacks a direct external carry-in control, so the two's complement behavior is achieved by pre-processing and careful design of the function stage and post-processing. Practically, one ALU control setting flips y (ny=1) while leaving zx and zy clear and selects addition (f=1); the post-processing and implicit handling inside the ALU produce the equivalent of adding one where needed. The provided assessment example lists control bits for x - y as zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=1 f=1 no=0. A concrete test you will run in the simulator sets x and y to small values and checks the result against subtraction performed in standard two's complement arithmetic. A common misconception is that subtraction requires a separate subtractor circuit; here you will see subtraction implemented by operand transformation and addition. When you write HDL tests, include negative and sign-boundary cases to confirm both numerical correctness and flag behavior for zero and negative results.

keyIdea.title: One adder, many ops
keyIdea.text: Subtraction is implemented by transforming inputs into two's complement form so the same adder hardware performs subtraction.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › x - y via addition

Two's complement trick

Use bitwise complement and addition to compute subtraction with the same adder hardware.

Mathematical identity
x - y = x + (~y + 1). Flip all bits of y and add one to get -y in two's complement.
ALU control example
One documented control combination for x - y is: zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=1 f=1 no=0. This flips y and uses addition.
Test vector
// Example test for x - y
x = 0b0000000000000100 // 4
y = 0b0000000000000011 // 3
controls: zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=1 f=1 no=0
// expected out = 0b0000000000000001 (1), zr=false, ng=false
Misconception

You do not need a dedicated subtractor. The ALU implements subtraction by transforming inputs and reusing the adder.

Key Takeaway

Verify subtraction with positive, negative and boundary cases to confirm both output and flag correctness.

screens.title: Memory Construction: From Bit to RAM16K
screens.narratorSegment: Memory in Project 2 is built recursively. Start with the Bit, a single 1-bit register with a load control that stores its value across ticks. Sixteen Bits compose a 16-bit Register that stores a word. RAM8 is created by grouping eight Registers and adding an address decoder that selects which register to read or write. To make RAM64 you combine eight RAM8 units and use higher address bits to select which RAM8 is active. This pattern repeats: RAM512 is eight RAM64s, RAM4K is eight RAM512s, and RAM16K is eight RAM4Ks. The recursive approach keeps design manageable: you test and trust each layer and reuse it to build the next. A concrete test: after constructing RAM64, write a non-zero value to an address in the second RAM8 block and confirm that reading addresses in other RAM8 blocks still yields zero. A frequent error is forgetting to isolate load signals when composing blocks; ensure the decoder gates load only for the selected submodule. Understanding the address bit partition—low bits select word within a block, high bits choose the block—is essential. This hierarchical design demonstrates how small, simple components scale into large memories.

keyIdea.title: Recursive assembly
keyIdea.text: Build larger RAMs by composing tested smaller blocks and decoding address bits to select the active submodule.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Memory Hierarchy

Bit → Register → RAM8 → ... → RAM16K

Grow memory by composing tested modules and partitioning address bits between block select and internal addressing.

Bit
1-bit storage with load control. Unit-test the hold and load behaviors.
Register
16 Bits wired together with a common load signal to form a word register.
RAM8
Eight Registers plus decoder logic to route load signals to a single selected register.
Address partitioning
Low bits index within a block; high bits select which block is active. For RAM64, low 3 bits pick a register and the next 3 bits pick the RAM8 block.
Concrete test

Write to an address in block 2 of RAM64 and confirm other blocks still read zero. This proves isolation and correct decoding.

Key Takeaway

Recursive composition keeps complexity manageable and testing localized to one level at a time.

screens.title: PC and Sequential Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: The Program Counter is a small sequential chip with three required behaviors: increment, load, and reset. Increment advances the counter by one each tick when enabled; load replaces the counter value with an externally supplied address when load is asserted; reset sets the counter to zero when reset is asserted. In HDL you will implement these behaviors with a register that accepts either the incremented value, the load input, or zero depending on control signals. A clear example: under normal execution the PC will increment; when a jump instruction requires branching, load=1 supplies a new address and the PC takes that value on the next tick. A common pitfall is failing to prioritize reset or load correctly so that simultaneous signals produce inconsistent behavior. The specification implies an explicit priority: reset typically forces zero regardless of other signals, and load usually overrides increment. For testing, write scenarios covering increment-only sequences, load operations from arbitrary values, and reset during a sequence to ensure the PC behaves deterministically. Understanding PC control is essential because it directly determines program flow in the von Neumann architecture.

narration.text: The Program Counter is a small sequential chip with three required behaviors: increment, load, and reset. Increment advances the counter by one each tick when enabled; load replaces the counter value with an externally supplied address when load is asserted; reset sets the counter to zero when reset is asserted. In HDL you will implement these behaviors with a register that accepts either the incremented value, the load input, or zero depending on control signals. A clear example: under normal execution the PC will increment; when a jump instruction requires branching, load=1 supplies a new address and the PC takes that value on the next tick. A common pitfall is failing to prioritize reset or load correctly so that simultaneous signals produce inconsistent behavior. The specification implies an explicit priority: reset typically forces zero regardless of other signals, and load usually overrides increment. For testing, write scenarios covering increment-only sequences, load operations from arbitrary values, and reset during a sequence to ensure the PC behaves deterministically. Understanding PC control is essential because it directly determines program flow in the von Neumann architecture.

keyIdea.title: Control priority
keyIdea.text: Define clear priority among reset, load and increment; tests must cover signal combinations to confirm deterministic behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Program Counter

PC: increment, load, reset

Design a register that selects among increment, load input, and reset value under clear priorities.

Increment behavior
When neither load nor reset is asserted, the PC increments by one each tick.
Load and reset
Load forces the PC to accept an external value; reset forces zero. Tests must verify these override increment when asserted.
Test cases
  • Sequence of increments from 0 to N.
  • Load a new value and then increment to confirm the new base.
  • Assert reset mid-sequence and confirm it returns to zero immediately.
Pitfall

Ambiguous signal priority can cause nondeterministic PC behavior. Explicitly define and test priorities in HDL.

Key Takeaway

Treat the PC as a small state machine; its correctness is required for reliable program flow and meaningful simulator runs.

screens.title: Testing Strategy and Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: A disciplined testing strategy keeps Project 2 manageable. For the ALU, plan tests that cover each of the 18 functions: pick representative x and y values and verify both the output bits and the zr/ng flags. Include tests that produce zero and negative outputs because flags are easy failure points. For R A M chips, verify three behaviors: uninitialized reads return zero, writes followed by reads at the same address return the written value, and writes to one address do not alter other addresses. Use low and high addresses across blocks to prove decoder correctness. For the PC test the increment sequence, the load action, and reset behavior under combinations. Concrete test scenario: write distinct sentinel values to addresses across RAM64's sub-blocks, then read each address and confirm only the targeted addresses hold their sentinels. Common mistakes include incorrect load gating when composing RAMs, wrong flag computation timing in the ALU, and inverted signal polarities for registers. Keep a debugging log that records failing tests, hypotheses, fixes, and the final passing verification; this log is part of the hands-on activity and helps you write the reflection comparing combinational and sequential design challenges.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Testing & Pitfalls

Testing strategy

Systematically exercise functions, flags, and address isolation with clear sentinel values and a debugging log.

ALU tests
Cover all 18 control combinations and check both output and zr/ng flags, including zero and negative edge cases.
RAM tests
Check uninitialized reads, write-then-read, and cross-address isolation with sentinel values across sub-blocks.
PC tests
Verify increment sequences, load-to-value behavior, and reset during sequences for deterministic control flow.
Debugging log sample
// Example log entry
Test: RAM64 write isolation
Failure: address 8 changed when writing to address 9
Hypothesis: decoder incorrectly gating load across blocks
Fix: adjust address bit split and gate load with high select
Result: pass
Common error

Not isolating load signals during composition causes writes to propagate to multiple registers. Ensure decoders gate the load to a single unit.

Key Takeaway

A short, well-structured test suite and a clear log reduce debugging time dramatically when composing larger chips.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three core ideas front of mind as you build Project 2. First, the ALU uses six control bits and three stages—pre-process, function, post-process—to implement eighteen functions and two status flags; implement and test the table rows methodically. Second, memory grows by recursion: test Bit and Register thoroughly, then assemble RAM8 and repeat to reach RAM16K; address bits partition into block selector and internal address. Third, testing and signal priorities matter: verify load gating in R A M and define PC priorities for reset, load and increment. A common learning point students miss is the difference between composing combinational logic and managing stateful, sequential behavior. Keep a debugging log, write clear unit tests, and reflect on which components challenged you more. Which chip required the most debugging, and how did feedback loops in registers change your design approach? That reflection is part of the project and cements understanding.

fullNarratorScript:
In this project you will produce the pieces that actually compute and retain data in the Hack computer. You will construct arithmetic components—half adder, full adder, a 16-bit adder and incrementer—and then assemble the ALU, which maps six control bits to eighteen functions. You will also build the memory hierarchy: a 1-bit storage element up through registers and layered R A M chips, finishing with RAM16K as the machine's data memory, and a program counter to sequence instructions. This work is central because it turns logic gates into operations and storage that together run programs. A concrete example: using the ALU you will implement addition and subtraction, and using the R A M chips you will store values that instructions read and update. A common misconception is that memory is a single monolithic block; in this project you will see how each level is constructed from the previous one and why that recursion matters for reliability and testability. By the end you’ll test every ALU function and verify read/write isolation across R A M addresses, and reflect on why sequential design requires a different mindset than combinational design.

These objectives guide your lab work and tests. First, you will complete Project 2 end-to-end: write HDL for every named chip, simulate it, and fix failing tests until each chip passes the provided scripts. Second, you will build the ALU and the memory chips—from the single Bit up to RAM16K—and you will show how each level composes into the next. Third, you'll verify hardware behavior: exhaust the ALU's 18 functions in the simulator and exercise R A M read/write patterns so you can prove address isolation and correct data persistence. Fourth, you will understand roles: know how the ALU implements operations and flags and how memory plus the program counter support the von Neumann execution model. Each objective emphasizes a skill: writing HDL, composing modules, testing with the simulator, and reasoning about sequential versus combinational design. A common pitfall is rushing to the largest chips without unit testing smaller blocks first; instead, verify each primitive and record your discoveries in a debugging log. These objectives prepare you both to build reliable hardware and to reason about why the components behave as they do.

Project work is safest when broken into verifiable milestones. Start by implementing and testing primitive arithmetic chips: HalfAdder and FullAdder. Move to 16-bit combinational modules: Add16 and Inc16, verifying carry propagation and increment edge cases. Implement the ALU last among combinational chips because it integrates many behaviors—verify all 18 functions listed in the specification table. For sequential work, implement Bit and then compose Register. Build RAM8 from Registers, then combine RAM8 units to form RAM64, RAM512, RAM4K and finally RAM16K. For the PC, check three behaviors: incrementing, loading a value when load is asserted, and resetting when reset is asserted. Testing strategy examples: for R A M, verify an uninitialized read returns 0, and that writing at one address does not alter other addresses. For the ALU, exercise combinations that produce zero and negative flags to validate status computation. A misconception to avoid is skipping unit tests for small chips; issues in large assemblies frequently trace back to an untested primitive. Track each passing test as a milestone toward project completion.

Project 2 names thirteen chips split into arithmetic and sequential groups. On the arithmetic side you will implement HalfAdder, FullAdder, Add16 and Inc16, and then integrate them into the ALU. Each smaller adder teaches a concrete idea: the HalfAdder shows how two bits sum and produce a carry; the FullAdder adds a carry input and demonstrates ripple carry when chained to form Add16. Inc16 reuses adder logic to perform a plus-one operation efficiently. The ALU then combines preprocessing and two function choices to produce complex behaviors. On the sequential side you will implement Bit and compose it into a 16-bit Register, then build RAM8 and grow it recursively through RAM64, RAM512, RAM4K to RAM16K. The PC is a small sequential special case that must increment, load, and reset correctly. A practical example: when you test RAM8, write the value 0b0000000000000011 to address 3 and then read it back; the value must persist only at address 3. A common misconception is that registers and R A M behave like immutable storage; in reality they hold state across clock cycles and require explicit load control to avoid unintentional overwrites. As you work, think of each chip as a contract: a precise HDL interface and tests that confirm the contract.

The ALU is specified as a table mapping six control bits to a set of functions and two status flags. The control bits are labeled zx, nx, zy, ny, f and no. These bits guide a three-stage computation: pre-process inputs x and y (zero and/or negate them), select a function (add or bitwise and), then post-process the result (possible negation). The ALU must also set zr if the output is zero and ng if the output is negative. Practically, this means each control combination implements a distinct arithmetic or logic operation such as zero, one, negative one, x, y, x+1, y-1, x-y and so on. A concrete example from the specification is the use of zx=1, nx=1, zy=1, ny=1, f=1, no=1 to produce the constant 1. A common misconception is to think the ALU has many separate circuits for each function; instead it reuses stages and input manipulation to cover many operations with the same hardware. When you build the ALU, focus on implementing the pre-processing controls correctly and verifying the table rows one by one in the simulator. Each passing row is strong evidence your composition matches the specification.

The ALU's pre-processing stage prepares inputs so a single function unit can produce many outcomes. The controls zx and zy force x or y to zero, which is useful when you want constants like zero, one, or negative one. The nx and ny bits negate the corresponding input, flipping every bit. Together these four bits let you compute complements, prepare operands for two's complement arithmetic, and create constant results without separate logic. For example, to produce -1 you can zero both inputs then negate the result appropriately through post-processing. A concrete example: to compute x - y using two's complement math, you will flip y with ny and use addition in the next stage; the pre-processing produces ~y so the function stage can add x and ~y. A common misunderstanding is that pre-processing merely cleans inputs; instead it encodes arithmetic tricks into operand transforms, enabling subtraction, increments, and constants with minimal hardware. When implementing this stage in HDL, be rigorous: write unit tests that assert the transformed x and y values for combinations of zx, nx, zy and ny so any mistake is caught before the function unit is exercised.

After pre-processing, the ALU must pick a function and possibly negate the result. The function bit f selects between arithmetic addition and bitwise AND. Addition composes the prepared operands into arithmetic results; AND performs bitwise masking operations. The post-processing control no negates the final output when needed, enabling further variety from a single data path. Equally important are the status flags: zr is set when the final output equals zero, and ng is set when the most significant bit is 1, indicating a negative two's complement number. For example, to produce a logical AND of original x and y, ensure zx and zy are cleared and f is 0; the result will reflect the bitwise intersection of the inputs. A common mistake is computing flags on the pre-processed value instead of the post-processed output; flags must reflect the value presented to the rest of the machine. When you implement this stage, add tests that check flag outcomes for edge cases like zero, negative one, and overflow-like patterns. Affirming flags are correct is crucial because later instruction logic depends on them for branches and comparisons.

A classic insight in Project 2 is implementing subtraction with addition through two's complement. The mathematical identity x - y = x + (~y + 1) means we can compute subtraction by flipping y's bits and adding one. The Hack ALU lacks a direct external carry-in control, so the two's complement behavior is achieved by pre-processing and careful design of the function stage and post-processing. Practically, one ALU control setting flips y (ny=1) while leaving zx and zy clear and selects addition (f=1); the post-processing and implicit handling inside the ALU produce the equivalent of adding one where needed. The provided assessment example lists control bits for x - y as zx=0 nx=0 zy=0 ny=1 f=1 no=0. A concrete test you will run in the simulator sets x and y to small values and checks the result against subtraction performed in standard two's complement arithmetic. A common misconception is that subtraction requires a separate subtractor circuit; here you will see subtraction implemented by operand transformation and addition. When you write HDL tests, include negative and sign-boundary cases to confirm both numerical correctness and flag behavior for zero and negative results.

Memory in Project 2 is built recursively. Start with the Bit, a single 1-bit register with a load control that stores its value across ticks. Sixteen Bits compose a 16-bit Register that stores a word. RAM8 is created by grouping eight Registers and adding an address decoder that selects which register to read or write. To make RAM64 you combine eight RAM8 units and use higher address bits to select which RAM8 is active. This pattern repeats: RAM512 is eight RAM64s, RAM4K is eight RAM512s, and RAM16K is eight RAM4Ks. The recursive approach keeps design manageable: you test and trust each layer and reuse it to build the next. A concrete test: after constructing RAM64, write a non-zero value to an address in the second RAM8 block and confirm that reading addresses in other RAM8 blocks still yields zero. A frequent error is forgetting to isolate load signals when composing blocks; ensure the decoder gates load only for the selected submodule. Understanding the address bit partition—low bits select word within a block, high bits choose the block—is essential. This hierarchical design demonstrates how small, simple components scale into large memories.

The Program Counter is a small sequential chip with three required behaviors: increment, load, and reset. Increment advances the counter by one each tick when enabled; load replaces the counter value with an externally supplied address when load is asserted; reset sets the counter to zero when reset is asserted. In HDL you will implement these behaviors with a register that accepts either the incremented value, the load input, or zero depending on control signals. A clear example: under normal execution the PC will increment; when a jump instruction requires branching, load=1 supplies a new address and the PC takes that value on the next tick. A common pitfall is failing to prioritize reset or load correctly so that simultaneous signals produce inconsistent behavior. The specification implies an explicit priority: reset typically forces zero regardless of other signals, and load usually overrides increment. For testing, write scenarios covering increment-only sequences, load operations from arbitrary values, and reset during a sequence to ensure the PC behaves deterministically. Understanding PC control is essential because it directly determines program flow in the von Neumann architecture.

A disciplined testing strategy keeps Project 2 manageable. For the ALU, plan tests that cover each of the 18 functions: pick representative x and y values and verify both the output bits and the zr/ng flags. Include tests that produce zero and negative outputs because flags are easy failure points. For R A M chips, verify three behaviors: uninitialized reads return zero, writes followed by reads at the same address return the written value, and writes to one address do not alter other addresses. Use low and high addresses across blocks to prove decoder correctness. For the PC test the increment sequence, the load action, and reset behavior under combinations. Concrete test scenario: write distinct sentinel values to addresses across RAM64's sub-blocks, then read each address and confirm only the targeted addresses hold their sentinels. Common mistakes include incorrect load gating when composing RAMs, wrong flag computation timing in the ALU, and inverted signal polarities for registers. Keep a debugging log that records failing tests, hypotheses, fixes, and the final passing verification; this log is part of the hands-on activity and helps you write the reflection comparing combinational and sequential design challenges.
